{{Short description|Ellipse tangent to all sides of a triangle}}
{{one source |date=May 2024}}
[[File:Inellipse-1.svg|thumb|Example of an inellipse]]
In [[triangle geometry]], an '''inellipse''' is an [[ellipse]] that touches the three sides of a [[triangle]]. The simplest example is the [[incircle]]. Further important inellipses are the [[Steiner inellipse]], which touches the triangle at the midpoints of its sides, the [[Mandart inellipse]] and [[Brocard inellipse]] (see [[#Examples|examples section]]). For any triangle there exist an infinite number of inellipses.

The Steiner inellipse plays a special role: Its area is the greatest of all inellipses.

Because a non-degenerate [[conic section]] is uniquely determined by five items out of the sets of vertices and tangents, in a triangle whose three sides are given as tangents one can specify only the points of contact on two sides. The third point of contact is then uniquely determined.

== Parametric representations, center, conjugate diameters ==
[[File:Inellipse-3.svg|thumb|An inellipse of a triangle is uniquely determined by the vertices of the triangle and two points of contact <math>U,V</math>.]]
The inellipse of the triangle with vertices 
:<math>O=(0,0), \; A=(a_1,a_2), \; B=(b_1,b_2) </math>
and points of contact
:<math>U=(u_1,u_2) ,\; V=(v_1,v_2) </math>
on <math>OA </math> and <math>OB</math> respectively can by described by the ''rational'' parametric representation
* <math>\left ( \frac{4u_1\xi^2+v_1ab}{4\xi^2+4\xi+ab},\frac{4u_2\xi^2+v_2ab}{4\xi^2+4\xi+ab}\right )\ , \ -\infty<\xi<\infty \ ,</math>
where <math> a,b </math> are uniquely determined by the choice of the points of contact:
:<math> a=\frac{1}{s-1}, \ u_i=s a_i,\quad b=\frac{1}{t-1}, \ v_i=t b_i \; ,\ 0<s,t<1 \; .</math>
The  ''third point of contact'' is
:<math>W= \left ( \frac{u_1a+v_1b}{a+b+2}\; ,\; \frac{u_2a+v_2b}{a+b+2}\right ) \; .</math>
The ''center'' of the inellipse is
:<math> M= \frac{ab}{ab-1}\left ( \frac{u_1+v_1}{2},\frac{u_2+v_2}{2}\right ) \; .</math>
The vectors
: <math>\vec f_1=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{ab}}{ab-1}\;(u_1+v_1,u_2+v_2)</math>
: <math>\vec f_2=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{ab}{ab-1}}\;(u_1-v_1,u_2-v_2)\; </math>
are two ''conjugate half diameters'' and the inellipse has the more common [[ellipse#Ellipse as an affine image of the unit circle x²+y²=1|''trigonometric '' parametric representation]]
* <math> \vec x = \vec{OM}+\vec f_1\cos \varphi + \vec f_2\sin \varphi \; .</math>
[[File:Inellipse-brianchon-pt.svg|thumb|Brianchon point <math>K</math>]]
The ''[[Brianchon's theorem|Brianchon point]] '' of the inellipse (common point <math>K</math> of the lines <math>\overline{AV} , \overline{BU}, \overline{OW}</math>) is
:<math>K: \left ( \frac{u_1a+v_1b}{a+b+1}\; ,\; \frac{u_2a+v_2b}{a+b+1}\right) \ .</math>

Varying <math> s,t </math> is an easy option to prescribe the two points of contact <math>U,V</math>. The given bounds for <math>s,t</math> guarantee that the points of contact are located on the sides of the triangle. They provide for <math>a,b</math> the bounds <math>-\infty<a,b<-1</math>.

''Remark:'' The parameters <math>a,b</math> are neither the semiaxes of the inellipse nor the lengths of two sides.

== Examples ==
[[File:Inellipse-mandart.svg|300px|thumb|Mandart inellipse]]

===Steiner inellipse===
For <math>s=t=\tfrac 1 2</math> the points of contact <math>U,V,W</math> are the midpoints of the sides and the inellipse is the [[Steiner inellipse]] (its center is the triangle's [[centroid]]).

===Incircle===
For <math> s=\tfrac{|OA|+|OB|-|AB|}{2|OA|},\; t=\tfrac{|OA|+|OB|-|AB|}{2|OB|}</math>
one gets the [[incircle]] of the triangle with center
:<math>\vec{OM}=\frac{|OB|\vec{OA}+|OA|\vec{OB}}{|OA|+|OB|+|AB|}\; .</math>

===Mandart inellipse===
For <math> s=\tfrac{|OA|-|OB|+|AB|}{2|OA|},\; t=\tfrac{-|OA|+|OB|+|AB|}{2|OB|}</math>
the inellipse is the ''Mandart inellipse'' of the triangle. It touches the sides at the points of contact of the [[excircle]]s (see diagram).
[[File:Inellipse-brocard.svg|300px|thumb|Brocard inellipse]]

===Brocard inellipse===
For <math> \ s=\tfrac{|OB|^2}{|OB|^2+|AB|^2}\; , \quad t=\tfrac{|OA|^2}{|OA|^2+|AB|^2}\; </math> 
one gets the ''Brocard inellipse''. It is uniquely determined by its Brianchon point given in ''[[trilinear coordinates]]'' <math>\ K: (|OB|:|OA|:|AB|)\ </math>.

== Derivations of the statements ==
[[File:Inellipse-2-ab.svg|thumb|500px|Determination of the inellipse by solving the problem for a hyperbola in an <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-plane and an additional transformation of the solution into the ''x''-''y''-plane.

<math>M</math> is the center of the sought inellipse and <math>D_1D_2,\; E_1E_2</math> two conjugate diameters.

In both planes the essential points are assigned by the same symbols. <math>g_\infty</math> is the line at infinity of the ''x''-''y''-plane.]]

;New coordinates:
For the proof of the statements one considers the task ''[[Projective plane|projectively]]'' and introduces convenient new inhomogene <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-coordinates such that the wanted conic section appears as a [[hyperbola]] and the points <math> U,V</math> become the points at infinity of the new coordinate axes. The points <math> A=(a_1,a_2),\; B=(b_1,b_2)</math> will be described in the new coordinate system by <math>A=[a,0], B=[0,b]</math> and the corresponding line has the equation <math>\frac \xi a + \frac \eta b =1 </math>. 
(Below it will turn out, that <math>a,b</math> have indeed the same meaning introduced in the statement above.) Now a hyperbola with the coordinate axes as asymptotes is sought, which touches the line <math>\overline{AB} </math>. This is an easy task. By a simple calculation one gets the hyperbola with the equation <math> \eta=\frac{ab}{4\xi}</math>. It touches the line <math>\overline{AB} </math> at point <math> W=[\tfrac{a}{2},\tfrac{b}{2}]</math>.

;Coordinate transformation:
The transformation of the solution into the ''x''-''y''-plane will be done using ''[[homogeneous coordinates]]'' and the matrix
:<math>\begin{bmatrix}
  u_1 & v_1 & 0 \\
  u_2 & v_2 & 0 \\
  1 & 1  & 1
  \end{bmatrix}\quad </math>.
A point <math>[x_1,x_2,x_3]</math> is mapped onto
:<math>\begin{bmatrix}
  u_1 & v_1 & 0 \\
  u_2 & v_2 & 0 \\
  1 & 1  & 1
  \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}u_1x_1+v_1x_2\\ 
               u_2x_1+v_2x_2\\
               x_1+x_2+x_3 \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \left( \frac{u_1x_1+v_1x_2}{ x_1+x_2+x_3}\; , \; \frac{u_2x_1+v_2x_2}{ x_1+x_2+x_3} \right ), \quad \text{if } x_1+x_2+x_3\ne0.</math>

A point <math>[\xi,\eta]</math> of the  <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-plane is represented by the column vector <math>[\xi,\eta,1]^T</math> (see [[homogeneous coordinates]]). A point at infinity is represented by <math>[\cdots,\cdots,0]^T</math>.

;Coordinate transformation of essential points:

:<math>U:\ [1,0,0]^T \ \rightarrow \ (u_1,u_2)\ , \quad V:\ [0,1,0]^T \ \rightarrow \ (v_1,v_2)\ , </math>
: <math>O: \ [0,0] \ \rightarrow \ (0,0) \ ,\quad A: \ [a,0] \rightarrow \ (a_1,a_2)\ , \quad B: \ [0,b] \rightarrow \ (b_1,b_2)\ ,</math>
:(One should consider: <math>\ a=\tfrac{1}{s-1}, \ u_i=s a_i,\quad b=\tfrac{1}{t-1}, \ v_i=t b_i \; </math>; see above.)
<math>g_\infty: \xi+\eta +1=0 \ </math> is the equation of the [[line at infinity]] of the ''x''-''y''-plane; its point at infinity is <math>[1,-1,0]^T</math>.
:<math>[1,-1,{\color{red}0}]^T \ \rightarrow \ (u_1-v_1,u_2-v_2,{\color{red}0})^T</math>
Hence the point at infinity of <math>g_\infty</math> (in <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-plane) is mapped onto a point at infinity of the ''x''-''y''-plane. That means: The two tangents of the hyperbola, which are parallel to  <math>g_\infty</math>, are parallel in the ''x''-''y''-plane, too. Their points of contact are

:<math> D_i: \left[\frac{\pm\sqrt{ab}}{2}, \frac{\pm\sqrt{ab}}{2}\right] \ \rightarrow \ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\pm\sqrt{ab}}{1\pm\sqrt{ab}}\;(u_1+v_1,u_2+v_2), \;</math>
Because the ellipse tangents at points <math>D_1,D_2</math> are parallel, the chord <math>D_1D_2</math> is a ''diameter'' and its midpoint the ''center''  <math>M</math> of the ellipse
:<math>M:\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{ab}{ab-1}\left (u_1+v_1,u_2+v_2\right ) \; .</math>
One easily checks, that <math>M</math> has the <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-coordinates
:<math>\ M: \; \left[\frac{-ab}{2},\frac{-ab}{2}\right]\; . </math>
In order to determine the diameter of the ellipse, which is conjugate to <math>D_1D_2</math>, in the <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-plane one has to determine the common points <math>E_1,E_2</math> of the hyperbola with the line through <math>M</math> parallel to the tangents (its equation is <math>\xi+\eta +ab=0</math>). One gets 
<math>E_i: \left[\tfrac{-ab\pm\sqrt{ab(ab-1)}}{2},\tfrac{-ab\mp\sqrt{ab(ab-1)}}{2}\right] </math>. And in ''x''-''y''-coordinates:
:<math>\ E_i=\frac{1}{2}\frac{ab}{ab-1}\left ( u_1+v_1,u_2+v_2\right ) \pm\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{ab(ab-1)}}{ab-1}\left (u_1-v_1,u_2-v_2\right )\; ,</math>
From the two conjugate diameters <math>D_1D_2,E_1E_2</math> there can be retrieved the two vectorial ''conjugate half diameters'' 
: <math>
\begin{align}
\vec f_1 & =\vec{MD_1}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{ab}}{ab-1}\;(u_1+v_1,u_2+v_2) \\[6pt]
\vec f_2 & =\vec{ME_1}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{ab}{ab-1}}\;(u_1-v_1,u_2-v_2)\;
\end{align}
</math>
and at least the ''trigonometric parametric representation'' of the inellipse:
:<math> \vec x = \vec{OM}+\vec f_1\cos \varphi + \vec f_2\sin \varphi \; .</math>

Analogously to the case of a [[Steiner ellipse#Determination of the semi axes and linear eccentricity|Steiner ellipse]] one can determine semiaxes, eccentricity, vertices, an equation in ''x''-''y''-coordinates and the area of the inellipse.

The  ''third touching point'' <math>W</math> on <math>AB</math> is:
:<math> W: \left[\frac{a}{2},\frac{b}{2} \right] \ \rightarrow \ \left( \frac{u_1a+v_1b}{a+b+2}\; ,\; \frac{u_2a+v_2b}{a+b+2}\right) \; .</math>

The ''Brianchon point'' of the inellipse is the common point <math>K</math> of the three lines <math>\overline{AV} , \overline{BU}, \overline{OW}</math>. In the <math>\xi</math>-<math>\eta</math>-plane these lines have the equations: <math> \xi=a\; ,\; \eta=b\; , \; a\eta-b\xi=0</math>. Hence point <math>K</math> has the coordinates:
:<math>K: \ [a,b] \ \rightarrow \ \left ( \frac{u_1a+v_1b}{a+b+1}\; ,\; \frac{u_2a+v_2b}{a+b+1}\right) \ .</math>
Transforming the hyperbola <math>\ \eta=\frac{ab}{4\xi}</math> yields the ''rational parametric representation'' of the inellipse:
:<math> \left[ \xi, \frac{ab}{4\xi} \right] \ \rightarrow \ \left( \frac{4u_1\xi^2+v_1ab}{4\xi^2+4\xi+ab},\frac{4u_2\xi^2+v_2ab}{4\xi^2+4\xi+ab}\right)\ , \ -\infty<\xi<\infty \ .</math>

;Incircle:
[[File:Inellipse-kreis.svg|thumb|Incircle of a triangle]]
For the incircle there is <math>|OU|=|OV|</math>, which is equivalent to
:'''(1)'''<math> \; s|OA|=t|OB|\; .\ </math> Additionally 
:'''(2)'''<math>\; (1-s)|OA|+(1-t)|OB| = |AB|</math>.  (see diagram)
Solving these two equations for <math>s,t</math> one gets
:'''(3)'''<math>\; s=\frac{|OA|+|OB|-|AB|}{2|OA|},\; t=\frac{|OA|+|OB|-|AB|}{2|OB|}\; .</math>
In order to get the coordinates of the center one firstly calculates using '''(1)''' und '''(3)'''
:<math>1 - \frac 1 {ab} = 1-(s-1)(t-1)=-st+s+t=\cdots=\frac{s}{2(|OB|}(|OA|+|OB|+|AB|)\; .</math>
Hence
:<math>\vec{OM}=\frac{|OB|}{s(|OA|+|OB|+|AB|)}\;(s\vec{OA}+t\vec{OB})=\cdots=\frac{|OB|\vec{OA}+|OA|\vec{OB}}{|OA|+|OB|+|AB|}\; .</math>

;Mandart inellipse
The parameters <math> s,t</math> for the Mandart inellipse can be retrieved from the properties of the points of contact (see [[:de:Ankreis#Berührpunktabstände|de: Ankreis]]).

;Brocard inellipse
The Brocard inellipse of a triangle is uniquely determined by its Brianchon point given in ''[[trilinear coordinates]]'' <math>\ K: (|OB|:|OA|:|AB|)\ </math>.<ref>Imre Juhász: ''Control point based representation of inellipses of triangles'', Annales Mathematicae et Informaticae
40 (2012) pp. 37–46, p.44</ref> Changing the trilinear coordinates into the more convenient representation <math>\ K: k_1\vec{OA}+k_2\vec{OB}\ </math> (see [[trilinear coordinates#Between Cartesian and trilinear coordinates|trilinear coordinates]]) yields <math>\ k_1=\tfrac{|OB|^2}{|OB|^2+|OA|^2+|AB|^2},\; k_2=\tfrac{|OA|^2}{|OB|^2+|OA|^2+|AB|^2}\ </math>. On the other hand, if the parameters <math>s,t</math> of an inellipse are given, one calculates from the formula above for <math>K</math>: <math>\ k_1=\tfrac{s(t-1)}{st-1},\; k_2=\tfrac{t(s-1)}{st-1}\ </math>. Equalizing both expressions for <math>k_1,k_2</math> and solving for <math>s,t</math> yields
:<math> s=\frac{|OB|^2}{|OB|^2+|AB|^2}\; , \quad t=\frac{|OA|^2}{|OA|^2+|AB|^2}\; .</math>

== Inellipse with the greatest area ==
*The ''Steiner inellipse'' has the greatest area of all inellipses of a triangle.

;Proof:
From [[ellipse#Theorem of Apollonios on conjugate diameters|Apollonios theorem]] on properties of conjugate semi diameters <math>\vec f_1,\vec f_2</math> of an ellipse one gets:

:<math>F=\pi\left|\det(\vec f_1,\vec f_2)\right|\quad </math> (see article on [[Steiner ellipse]]).

For the inellipse with parameters <math>s,t</math> one gets
:<math>\det(\vec f_1,\vec f_2)
=\frac{1}{4}\frac{ab}{(ab-1)^{3/2}}\det(s\vec a+t \vec b,s\vec a-t \vec b)</math>
:::::<math>=\frac{1}{2}\frac{s\sqrt{s-1}\;t\sqrt{t-1}}{(1-(s-1)(t-1))^{3/2}}\det(\vec b,\vec a)\; , </math>
where <math>\vec a=(a_1,a_2), \; \vec b=(b_1,b_2),\;\vec u=(u_1,u_2), \vec v=(v_1,v_2),\; \vec u=s\vec a,\; \vec v=t\vec b</math>. <br>
In order to omit the roots, it is enough to investigate the [[Maxima and minima|extrema]] of function <math>G(s,t)=\tfrac{s^2(s-1)\;t^2(t-1)}{(1-(s-1)(t-1))^3}</math>:
:<math> G_s=0 \ \rightarrow \ 3s-2+2(s-1)(t-1)=0\; . </math>
Because <math>G(s,t)=G(t,s)</math> one gets from the exchange of ''s'' and ''t'':
:<math> G_t=0\ \rightarrow \ 3t-2+2(s-1)(t-1)=0\; . </math>
Solving both equations for ''s'' and ''t'' yields
:<math> s=t=\frac{1}{2}\; ,\quad</math> which are the parameters of the Steiner inellipse.
